intro.what: Thinking Profile helps you plan a whole unit around one kind of thinking, so students practise it in four to six tasks and can see for themselves that they are getting better.
intro.why_unit: A single task shows that students can do their own thinking with AI in the room. A whole unit shows them that they are getting better at it: they meet the same ladder four to six times and watch themselves climb.
intro.retell: I followed Causes and systems through our ecosystems unit, and my students climbed from step 1 to step 3.

not_graded: The ladder is for students' own self-check. It is never graded.
honesty: The ladders are Choosewise's own, built on the logic of the SOLO taxonomy. They have not been tested in research.

questions: Which step did my answer reach?
What in my answer shows it?

rules: At least half of the tasks in the plan come from the followed cluster's preferred tasks.
A task from another cluster may be borrowed only when its content makes students use the followed cluster's thinking.
Repeating the same task is intended when each round has harder inputs: more variables, less familiar content or less support.
Demand rises across the unit, so the later tasks give room to reach steps 3 and 4.
Students rate every task on the followed cluster's ladder, whatever tool the task came from.
regulating_rule: Students rate the ladder on the Think back part at the end of each task, not on the task answer.
rules_regulating: Any task from any tool may be used, because every task ends with a Think back step.
Repeating the same task is intended when each round has harder inputs: more variables, less familiar content or less support.

Students rate the ladder on the Think back part at the end of each task, not on the task answer.

ladders.in_class: Students solve one problem in as many different ways as they can, then hunt for the most unusual way.

steps.text: I write down one idea that works.
steps.shows: Point to the idea and to what makes it work.

steps.text: I write down several ideas that work in different ways, not small changes of the same idea.
steps.shows: Point to each idea and to what makes it different from the others.

steps.text: I sort my ideas into kinds and add one from a kind I had missed.
steps.shows: Point to your groups, their names and the idea you added to fill the gap.

steps.text: I pick the idea that fits best when one condition changes, explain why, and say how sure I am.
steps.shows: Point to the changed condition, the idea you picked, your reason and the words that say how sure you are.

ladders.in_class: Students set criteria or say what evidence would convince them before they decide, then defend their choice against the other side.

steps.text: I make a choice or a judgement and give one reason for it.
steps.shows: Point to your choice and the one reason.

steps.text: I give several reasons, each backed by a fact or a rule I can check.
steps.shows: Point to each reason and the fact or rule beside it.

steps.text: I weigh my reasons against each other and against the other side, and show which one decides it.
steps.shows: Point to where you answer the other side and the sentence that says which reason weighs most.

steps.text: I test my judgement on a new case or a new piece of evidence, and say how sure I am.
steps.shows: Point to the new case or evidence, whether your judgement held, and the words that say how sure you are.

ladders.in_class: Students set two cases side by side, map what matches, write the rule the comparison shows and try it on a new case.

steps.text: I name one thing the two cases share.
steps.shows: Point to the shared feature in both cases.

steps.text: I name several things that match and at least one place where the cases differ.
steps.shows: Point to each match and to the difference.

steps.text: I explain the rule that makes the cases match, and where the comparison breaks.
steps.shows: Point to the sentence that states the rule and to the place where the comparison breaks.

steps.text: I use the rule on a new case, and say how sure I am that it fits.
steps.shows: Point to the new case, your rule used on it, and the words that say how sure you are.

ladders.in_class: Students explain a puzzling result, rebuild a rule from what they know for certain, or estimate and model a real question, saying every assumption out loud.

steps.text: I give one explanation or one fact I know for certain.
steps.shows: Point to the explanation or the fact.

steps.text: I give several explanations or steps, and say what each one rests on.
steps.shows: Point to each explanation or step and what it rests on: evidence, a known fact or an assumption.

steps.text: I link my steps into one line of reasoning, or show which explanation fits the evidence best.
steps.shows: Point to the linking words (because, so, which means) or to the evidence that rules out the other explanations.

steps.text: I use my reasoning on a new case or a changed number, say where it stops working, and say how sure I am.
steps.shows: Point to the new case, the place where your reasoning stops working, and the words that say how sure you are.

ladders.in_class: Students follow a decision through its consequences, or draw how the parts of a system affect each other and find the loops.

steps.text: I name one cause and one effect.
steps.shows: Point to the cause, the effect and the word that links them.

steps.text: I build a chain: A leads to B leads to C.
steps.shows: Point to each link in the chain: at least three parts in a row.

steps.text: I find a loop: C affects A again, or a delay or a side effect.
steps.shows: Point to the arrow or sentence that leads back to the start, or that names the delay or side effect.

steps.text: I use the loop to predict what happens if one part changes, and say how sure I am.
steps.shows: Point to the part you changed, your prediction and the words that say how sure you are.

ladders.in_class: At the end of any task, students write for two minutes about how they thought, not what they found, and what they would do differently.

steps.text: I name one thing I did while I worked.
steps.shows: Point to the strategy you name, such as "I drew it". "I thought harder" does not count.

steps.text: I describe several steps in how I worked, and one moment that shaped how I worked, such as changing my approach or getting stuck.
steps.shows: Point to each step and to the moment that shaped how you worked.

steps.text: I explain what made me change my approach or moved me on, and why it helped.
steps.shows: Point to the sentence that says what made you change your approach or moved you on, and why it helped.

steps.text: I say what I would change next time and why, and how sure I am that it would help.
steps.shows: Point to what you would change, your reason and the words that say how sure you are.

example.subject: Biology
example.thread: One question runs through the unit: when one thing in an ecosystem changes, what else changes, and when? Each week students follow the effects a little further: a chain in week 1, a loop in week 2, a delayed side effect in week 3, and by week 6 a prediction they back with the loop.

plan.what: Queensland, 1935: cane toads are released to eat the beetles that damage sugar cane. Students write the first consequence, the consequence of that, and one more.
inputs: What is the lesson about?: Food chains and what happens when a new species is introduced: the cane toads released in Queensland in 1935 to control cane beetles
What do students already know?: Producers, consumers and simple food chains

plan.what: Students draw how snowshoe hares, lynx and the shrubs the hares eat affect each other, find one loop and say whether it grows or balances itself.
inputs: What is the lesson about?: Predators and prey: snowshoe hares, lynx and the shrubs the hares eat in the Canadian forest, whose numbers rise and fall in a cycle of about ten years
What do students already know?: Food chains and food webs; the cane toad chain from week 1

plan.what: Harder inputs: a farmer spreads extra fertiliser next to a lake. Students follow the chain into the water and find the delayed side effect: algae bloom, die and rot, and the fish run short of oxygen.
inputs: What is the lesson about?: Nutrients in a lake ecosystem: a farmer spreads extra fertiliser on a field next to a lake to grow more wheat
What do students already know?: Food webs, photosynthesis, and that decomposers break down dead material

plan.what: Borrowed from Explaining. 29 reindeer released on St. Matthew Island in 1944 grew to about 6,000 by 1963, then fell to 42 by 1966. Students propose explanations and say what evidence would tell them apart. Researchers still disagree: overgrazed lichen plus a hard winter, or the winter alone.
inputs: What is the lesson about?: Population growth and crashes: the reindeer on St. Matthew Island, Alaska, which grew from 29 in 1944 to about 6,000 in 1963 and fell to 42 by 1966
What do students already know?: Food webs, predator and prey loops, and that a population needs enough food to survive the winter

plan.what: Borrowed from Comparing. Two identical forests have too many deer, and both remove the same number every year. In A most of the deer removed are females, in B most are males. Students compare what happens, write the rule and predict a third forest.
inputs: How hard should the difference be to see?: Easier to see
What is the lesson about?: Managing a population: two forests with too many deer that remove the same number of deer each year, mostly females in one forest and mostly males in the other
What do students already know?: Birth and death rates, predator and prey loops, and the St. Matthew Island reindeer crash

plan.what: Back to the hares, now with less support: a disease halves the lynx. Students use their loop to predict what happens to hares and shrubs over the next few years, and say how sure they are.
inputs: What is the lesson about?: Predicting change in an ecosystem: a disease halves the lynx in a forest with snowshoe hares and the shrubs they eat. What happens to the hares and the shrubs over the next few years?
What do students already know?: The hare and lynx loop from week 2, delays and side effects from week 3, and the deer comparison from week 5

example.tell_students: For six weeks we practise one kind of thinking: causes and systems. After every task you check your answer against the same four-step ladder, point to the words that show your step, and write your next step. Nobody grades the ladder. It is there so you can see yourself climb.
example.students_note: Fictional examples: two Grade 8 answers to the week 4 task, each with the student's own self-check.

students.name: Amira
students.answer: There were no wolves on the island, so nothing killed the reindeer and there got to be too many. They ate all the lichen, so there was no food left, so they starved. Maybe some of them also got a disease.
students.shows: No predators, then too many reindeer, then they ate the lichen, then they starved. That is four parts in a row.
students.next: Find the arrow that goes back: what eating the lichen did to the reindeer the year after.

students.name: Theo
students.answer: More reindeer ate more lichen, and less lichen meant less food for the reindeer, so it is a loop. But lichen grows back really slowly, so the herd kept growing for years after the food started running out. Then one very bad winter with deep snow finished them off. If it was only the winter, they would have been fat and healthy in 1963. If it was the food, they would already be getting thinner. Weighing the reindeer from before the crash would tell us which.
students.shows: The loop is "less lichen meant less food for the reindeer". The delay is "lichen grows back really slowly".
students.next: Use the loop to predict something, like what would happen if only ten reindeer had been released, and say how sure I am.

evidence.label: strong
evidence.text: Teaching students to plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning adds +8 months of progress on average in the EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit, based on 355 studies, with 4 of 5 padlocks for the strength of the evidence. The EEF adds that this impact can be hard to realise in practice: teachers need to teach the strategies explicitly and build them into lessons.

sources.text: EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit: Metacognition and self-regulation

evidence.label: promising
evidence.text: In a meta-analysis of classrooms from Grade 3 to Grade 12, students who scored their own work did better on later tests than students who did not (Sanchez et al. 2017, g = 0.34), though 12 of the 44 effects were negative. Students' own ratings agree only partly with other measures of their work, with correlations from about 0.2 to 0.8 (as summarised by Andrade 2019). There is some evidence they agree more when the criteria are concrete and task-specific and students are trained to use them (Andrade 2019), which is why every step names something students can point to.

sources.text: Sanchez, Atkinson, Koenka, Moshontz & Cooper 2017, Journal of Educational Psychology

evidence.label: framework
evidence.text: The ladders are Choosewise's own, built on the logic of the SOLO taxonomy. They have not been tested in research. SOLO describes how the quality of an answer grows; it is not evidence that these ladders improve students' thinking.

sources.text: Biggs & Collis 1982, Evaluating the Quality of Learning: The SOLO Taxonomy
